title: Israel and Judah
subtitle: 1,200–586 BC · From Merneptah's Stele to the Babylonian Exile

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Highland settlement, a contested United Monarchy, and two divided kingdoms

entries.label: The Merneptah Stele Names "Israel"
entries.hint: An Egyptian victory inscription of Pharaoh Merneptah, listing peoples and places subdued in Canaan, includes the line "Israel is laid waste, its seed is not" — written with the hieroglyphic determinative for a people rather than a city-state, this is the earliest known reference to Israel by any name, confirming that a group identified as Israel existed in the Canaanite highlands by the late 13th century BC, though the inscription says nothing about its size, organisation or origins.
entries.note: Merneptah Stele (Cairo Egyptian Museum, JE 31408), line 27, c.1208 BC; the sole extrabiblical attestation of "Israel" from this early period.

entries.label: New Highland Villages, Contested Origins
entries.hint: Archaeological survey has identified several hundred small, unfortified new settlements appearing across the central highlands between roughly 1200 and 1050 BC, marked by four-room houses, collared-rim storage jars and an absence of pig bones — but their origin is genuinely disputed among specialists, read variously as Israelite tribes arriving from outside Canaan, indigenous Canaanite peasants and pastoralists resettling the highlands, or some combination, with no consensus that the biblical conquest narrative in Joshua describes the process as it actually happened.
entries.note: Archaeological survey synthesis (I. Finkelstein and others) on central highland settlement patterns, Iron Age I; conquest, peaceful-infiltration and internal-emergence models remain actively debated.

entries.label: Saul, a First King
entries.hint: The biblical narrative presents Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin, as Israel's first king, raised up to unify the tribes against Philistine pressure and reigning from Gibeah near Jerusalem — no contemporary inscription or excavated royal structure has been securely tied to Saul himself, so his reign is known only through later biblical narrative, making it the least externally verifiable of the United Monarchy's three kings.
entries.note: 1 Samuel 9–31; no extrabiblical attestation of Saul has been identified to date.

entries.label: David and a Disputed "House of David"
entries.hint: The Tel Dan Stele, an Aramaic victory inscription of a 9th-century BC Damascene king boasting of killing a king of "the House of David" (bytdwd), is widely accepted — including by scholars otherwise skeptical of the biblical narrative — as confirming that David was a real historical figure and dynastic founder within a century of his traditional reign; what remains genuinely contested is the scale of David's own kingdom, since Jerusalem's 10th-century BC archaeological footprint is modest and no consensus exists on whether he ruled a substantial state or a smaller highland chiefdom later magnified in national memory.
entries.note: Tel Dan Stele fragments A and B (Israel Museum), discovered 1993–1994, line 9: bytdwd ("House of David"); the earliest extrabiblical reference to David, roughly a century after his traditional reign.

entries.label: Solomon and the Temple Tradition
entries.hint: Biblical tradition credits Solomon, David's son, with vast wealth, an extensive building programme including Jerusalem's First Temple, and a kingdom stretching from the Euphrates to Egypt's border — claims no surviving contemporary inscription confirms, and archaeologists are divided over whether monumental gate structures at Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer conventionally dated to his reign truly belong to it or to a later Omride building programme a century afterward, leaving Solomon's historical footprint considerably harder to fix than his son's kingdom's subsequent, better-attested fracture.
entries.note: 1 Kings 3–11; the "Solomonic gates" attribution at Megiddo/Hazor/Gezer versus a 9th-century Omride redating is an unresolved stratigraphic and chronological debate.

entries.label: Omri Founds a Dynasty Named for Him
entries.hint: Omri, a military commander who seized the northern throne after a civil war, built a new capital at Samaria on a previously unoccupied hill and founded a dynasty so internationally prominent that Assyrian inscriptions continued to call the kingdom of Israel "the House of Omri" for more than a century after his own line was violently overthrown — the biblical text, in sharp contrast, gives Omri only a few dismissive verses despite his evident historical importance.
entries.note: 1 Kings 16:21–28; Assyrian royal inscriptions (Shalmaneser III onward) referring to Israel as Bit-Ḫumri, "House of Omri," into the reign of Jehu and beyond.

entries.label: Ahab and a Tyrian Marriage
entries.hint: Ahab, Omri's son, expanded Samaria's building programme and, through marriage to Jezebel, daughter of the king of Tyre, secured a Phoenician alliance that brought commercial prosperity alongside sustained biblical condemnation for the Baal worship it introduced at court — his reign's genuine military strength is independently confirmed by Assyrian records rather than by the biblical text, which focuses almost entirely on his religious conflict with the prophet Elijah.
entries.note: 1 Kings 16:29–22:40; the Tyrian marriage alliance also appears in Josephus, Antiquities 8.13.1–2, citing the Phoenician historian Menander of Ephesus.

entries.label: Jehu's Bloody Coup
entries.hint: Jehu, a chariot commander anointed by a prophet's messenger, seized the throne by personally killing King Joram and orchestrating the massacre of the entire House of Omri along with Baal's priesthood — a coup the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III commemorated within his own lifetime by depicting Jehu (or his envoy) bowing in submission on the Black Obelisk, an extraordinary case of a biblical figure's own generation leaving an independent, dateable visual record.
entries.note: 2 Kings 9–10; Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (British Museum, ME 118885), register 2, labelled "Jehu, son of Omri" — a genealogical error, since Jehu ended Omri's line rather than continuing it, but the identification of the submitting king as Jehu is accepted.

entries.label: A Kingdom's Final, Unstable Decades
entries.hint: Israel's last generation saw four kings assassinated in rapid succession amid Assyrian pressure, with the biblical text itself remarking on the political chaos — Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah and Pekah each held the throne only briefly before the kingdom's final king, Hoshea, was reduced to an Assyrian vassal and then imprisoned for seeking Egyptian support, precipitating the siege that ended the northern kingdom altogether.
entries.note: 2 Kings 15:8–17:6; five kings across roughly three decades, several removed by assassination, reflecting acute internal instability under mounting Assyrian pressure.

entries.label: Hezekiah's Religious and Military Stand
entries.hint: Hezekiah centralised worship at the Jerusalem Temple, removing rival shrines and cultic objects including a bronze serpent attributed to Moses, while preparing Jerusalem militarily and hydraulically for the Assyrian confrontation his rebellion against tribute invited — his reign is the best externally corroborated of any Judahite king before Josiah, attested independently in Assyrian royal annals as well as the biblical narrative.
entries.note: 2 Kings 18:1–20:21; Sennacherib's Annals (Taylor Prism, British Museum) corroborate Hezekiah's reign and rebellion from the Assyrian side.

entries.label: Josiah's Reform and Sudden Death
entries.hint: Josiah, crowned at age eight after his father's assassination, launched Judah's most sweeping religious centralisation during a Temple renovation that produced a "Book of the Law" — prompting the destruction of rival shrines across Judah and formerly Israelite territory — before dying at Megiddo in a confrontation with Pharaoh Necho II, an abrupt end that historians increasingly treat as more likely a summons gone wrong or a minor skirmish than the pitched battle later tradition remembered.
entries.note: 2 Kings 22:1–23:30; 2 Chronicles 35:20–24, on Josiah's death at Megiddo confronting Necho II, 609 BC.

entries.label: Judah's Last Kings under Empire
entries.hint: In the seventeen years after Josiah's death, Judah cycled through four kings installed and deposed by competing Egyptian and Babylonian overlords — Jehoahaz removed by Necho within three months, Jehoiakim and then the eighteen-year-old Jehoiachin deported by Nebuchadnezzar II, and finally Zedekiah, whose own rebellion brought Jerusalem's final destruction — a kingdom whose throne by its last decade was entirely at the disposal of foreign empires.
entries.note: 2 Kings 23:31–25:7; Babylonian Chronicle (BM 21946) independently confirms Nebuchadnezzar II's capture of Jerusalem and the 597 BC deportation, naming "the king of Judah" (Jehoiachin) among those taken.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Qarqar, Jehu's coup, the fall of Samaria, and two sieges of Jerusalem

entries.label: Ahab's Chariots at Qarqar
entries.hint: Shalmaneser III's own inscription of the Battle of Qarqar lists a coalition of Levantine states resisting Assyrian expansion, crediting "Ahab the Israelite" with contributing two thousand chariots — the largest chariot contingent of any coalition member and independent confirmation that Ahab's kingdom, however brief its scriptural treatment, commanded real regional military weight.
entries.note: Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III (British Museum, ME 118884), c.853 BC, listing Ahab of Israel's chariot contribution to the anti-Assyrian coalition at Qarqar.

entries.label: The Fall of Samaria
entries.hint: After a three-year siege begun under Shalmaneser V and completed under Sargon II, Samaria fell and the kingdom of Israel ceased to exist as a state, with tens of thousands of its inhabitants deported to Mesopotamia and Media and replaced by populations resettled from elsewhere in the Assyrian empire — the biblical and Assyrian accounts disagree on which king gets credit for the final capture, but agree closely on the scale and permanence of the deportation.
entries.note: 2 Kings 17:3–6; Sargon II's Nimrud Prism and Khorsabad Annals both claim credit for Samaria's capture and record deporting 27,290 people — the historical basis for the later "Ten Lost Tribes" tradition.

entries.label: Sennacherib's Siege of Jerusalem
entries.hint: Sennacherib's own annals claim he shut Hezekiah up "like a caged bird" in Jerusalem after devastating Judah's countryside and capturing forty-six fortified towns, while the biblical account frames the siege's end as a sudden, unexplained Assyrian withdrawal and near-miraculous deliverance — both sources agree Jerusalem itself was not taken and that Hezekiah paid a heavy tribute, a rare case where accounts from both belligerents survive and can be read side by side, even though they interpret the outcome in opposite terms.
entries.note: Sennacherib's Annals (Taylor Prism, British Museum, and Oriental Institute Prism); 2 Kings 18:13–19:37; Lachish reliefs (British Museum) depict the Assyrian side of the same 701 BC campaign at the Judahite city of Lachish.

entries.label: The First Deportation
entries.hint: Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylonian Chronicle records capturing Jerusalem, seizing its king and installing a replacement of his own choosing — matching the biblical account of King Jehoiachin's deportation to Babylon along with the royal court, craftsmen and Temple treasures, a first, smaller exile eleven years before the city's final destruction.
entries.note: Babylonian Chronicle (BM 21946), entry for Nebuchadnezzar II's seventh year (597 BC); 2 Kings 24:10–17.

entries.label: The Destruction of Jerusalem
entries.hint: After an eighteen-month siege provoked by Zedekiah's rebellion against Babylonian overlordship, Nebuchadnezzar II's forces breached Jerusalem's walls, burned the Temple and royal palace, dismantled the city's fortifications and deported a further substantial portion of the population, ending both the kingdom of Judah's political existence and the First Temple period.
entries.note: 2 Kings 25:1–21; Jeremiah 39, 52; archaeological destruction layers at Jerusalem's City of David and Temple Mount vicinity dated to this campaign.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Royal storage jars and Josiah's centralizing reform

entries.label: The lmlk Storage-Jar System
entries.hint: Thousands of large storage-jar handles stamped "lmlk" ("belonging to the king") alongside one of four place names and a two-winged or four-winged emblem have been excavated across Judah, evidence of a centralised royal system for collecting, storing and redistributing agricultural surplus — almost certainly wine and oil — most heavily concentrated in the reign of Hezekiah and plausibly connected to provisioning against the anticipated Assyrian siege of 701 BC.
entries.note: Over 2,000 lmlk-stamped jar handles catalogued from Judahite sites, concentrated stratigraphically around the late 8th century BC; exact administrative purpose (taxation, military provisioning, or both) still debated.

entries.label: Josiah Centralises Worship at Jerusalem
entries.hint: Following the discovery of a law scroll during Temple repairs, Josiah convened Judah's elders, had the text read publicly, and used it to justify destroying rural shrines ("high places") throughout Judah and former Israelite territory, executing their priests and concentrating sacrificial worship exclusively at the Jerusalem Temple — a religious reform enacted through direct royal administrative power, reorganising the kingdom's cultic geography in a single sustained campaign.
entries.note: 2 Kings 22:3–23:20; most historians identify the scroll, wholly or in part, with an early form of Deuteronomy, though the identification and the account's own composition are debated.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Yahwism's development, prophets, and evidence for a less settled early religion

entries.label: Elijah's Confrontation with Baal Worship
entries.hint: The prophet Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal at Mount Carmel, set during Ahab and Jezebel's reign, frames the introduction of Tyrian Baal worship at the Israelite court as a national crisis requiring decisive prophetic intervention — a foundational narrative for the developing conviction, not yet uniformly held across Israelite society, that Yahweh alone, and no other god, was to be worshipped.
entries.note: 1 Kings 18:1–46; read alongside the Kuntillet Ajrud evidence, the narrative reflects a religious struggle over exclusive Yahwism that was still unresolved among ordinary worshippers well into the following century.

entries.label: "Yahweh and His Asherah"
entries.hint: Hebrew inscriptions on storage jars at a remote Sinai waystation invoke blessings from "Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah" and "Yahweh of Teman and his Asherah," pairing Israel's national god with a consort figure otherwise associated with Canaanite religion — evidence, hard to reconcile with later strict monotheism, that popular Israelite religious practice in the 9th–8th centuries BC was considerably closer to its broader Canaanite context than the Hebrew Bible's own retrospective, idealised presentation suggests.
entries.note: Kuntillet Ajrud pithoi inscriptions, Israel Antiquities Authority, c.800 BC; interpretation of "Asherah" as a consort goddess versus a cultic object remains debated among epigraphers.

entries.label: Isaiah and the Fate of Jerusalem
entries.hint: The prophet Isaiah, active during the Assyrian crises of Ahaz's and Hezekiah's reigns, combined sharp condemnation of social injustice and royal foreign-policy choices with an influential theological claim that Jerusalem, as Yahweh's chosen city, would not ultimately fall — a claim events of 701 BC seemed to confirm and that later shaped Judahite political theology, complicating the reckoning required when the city did fall in 586 BC.
entries.note: Isaiah 1–39 (First Isaiah), dated by most scholars substantially to the 8th century BC reflecting the Assyrian-era crises.

entries.label: Jeremiah's Warnings before the Fall
entries.hint: The prophet Jeremiah spent decades warning Judah's last kings that rebellion against Babylon would bring destruction, was imprisoned and threatened with death for counselling surrender, and lived to see Jerusalem fall exactly as he had predicted — a career whose surviving oracles, alongside the Book of Lamentations traditionally associated with him, provide some of the most emotionally direct ancient testimony to a kingdom's final collapse.
entries.note: Jeremiah 1–45; the Lachish Letters (see Lives) independently corroborate the atmosphere of military desperation and prophetic activity Jeremiah's book describes in Judah's final years.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Lachish reliefs and the everyday epigraphy of Hebrew seals

entries.label: The Lachish Reliefs
entries.hint: Carved to decorate Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh, an extensive relief cycle depicts the Assyrian siege and capture of Lachish, Judah's second city, in vivid narrative detail — siege ramps, battering rams, deportees, impaled prisoners and Sennacherib himself receiving submission — the single most detailed ancient visual record of any Judahite city, created not by Judahites but by the empire that destroyed it, for its own commemorative purposes.
entries.note: Lachish reliefs from Sennacherib's Southwest Palace, Nineveh (British Museum, ME 124906–124915), c.700–681 BC.

entries.label: Personal Seals and Bullae
entries.hint: Hundreds of small stone seals and clay bullae (seal impressions) bearing personal names in Hebrew script, often with patronymics and occasionally with titles such as "servant of the king," survive from Judahite administrative contexts — a handful bear names matching, though not certainly identifying, figures known from the biblical text, offering a rare glimpse of an ordinary Judahite bureaucratic culture of literate individual identity beneath the royal narrative.
entries.note: Comparative corpus of Judahite personal seals and bullae, 8th–6th century BC, including examples from the City of David excavations, Jerusalem.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Siloam Inscription and the Deuteronomistic History's composition

entries.label: The Siloam Inscription
entries.hint: Carved into the rock wall of Hezekiah's water tunnel to commemorate its completion, this six-line Hebrew inscription describes, from the workers' own perspective, the moment two teams digging from opposite ends heard each other's picks through the rock and met — one of the longest and most securely dated ancient Hebrew inscriptions, and a rare technical, non-royal, non-religious voice from Judah's own workforce.
entries.note: Siloam Inscription (Istanbul Archaeology Museums), from Hezekiah's Tunnel, Jerusalem, c.700 BC.

entries.label: A History Taking Shape under the Kings
entries.hint: Most scholars locate a major stage in composing the continuous narrative running from Joshua through Kings — later called the Deuteronomistic History — to the reign of Josiah or the early exile, when court and Temple scribes shaped inherited traditions, royal annals and prophetic accounts into a connected history judging each king by loyalty to centralised, exclusive Yahwism; the work is therefore best read as retrospective theological history compiled centuries after the events its earliest chapters describe, not a contemporary chronicle.
entries.note: The Deuteronomistic History hypothesis (M. Noth and subsequent scholarship); composition history, authorship and dating remain actively debated, with most models placing significant redaction in the late 7th or 6th century BC.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Highland agriculture and the royal lmlk storage-jar system

entries.label: Terracing, Olives and Wine
entries.hint: The Israelite and Judahite highland economy rested on labour-intensive stone terracing that converted steep, thin-soiled slopes into cultivable land for olives, grapes and cereals, alongside small-scale animal husbandry — an agricultural base inherited largely unchanged from earlier Canaanite practice, whose oil and wine surplus, gathered and stored through systems like the royal lmlk jars, funded the two kingdoms' administrations and trade.
entries.note: Archaeological survey of Iron Age agricultural terracing and installations (wine and oil presses) across the central highlands, continuous from Late Bronze Canaanite antecedents.

entries.label: The Samaria Ostraca
entries.hint: A cache of inked potsherds from the royal storehouse at Samaria records shipments of wine and oil from named estates and clans to the crown, using a dating system tied to the king's regnal years — a direct administrative snapshot of the Israelite tax-in-kind system feeding the royal court, written in ordinary practical Hebrew rather than royal inscription or biblical narrative.
entries.note: Samaria Ostraca (c.784–748 BC, Israel Antiquities Authority and Harvard Semitic Museum), c.100 legible administrative dockets.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Hezekiah's tunnel, engineered against a coming siege

entries.label: Hezekiah's Tunnel
entries.hint: Anticipating an Assyrian siege, Hezekiah's engineers cut a 533-metre channel through solid bedrock to redirect the Gihon Spring's water inside Jerusalem's walls to the Siloam Pool, digging from both ends simultaneously along a winding, non-obvious path and meeting near the middle — a striking feat of ancient surveying and tunnelling executed under real strategic time pressure, commemorated by the workers themselves in the Siloam Inscription.
entries.note: Hezekiah's Tunnel (Siloam Tunnel), Jerusalem, c.701 BC; 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: A Tyrian marriage alliance, and small states between empires

entries.label: An Israelite-Tyrian Alliance
entries.hint: Ahab's marriage to Jezebel, daughter of the Tyrian king Ithobaal I, sealed a commercial and political alliance between Israel and Phoenicia's leading maritime power, opening Israelite access to Mediterranean trade networks and Phoenician craftsmanship (reflected in the biblical description of an "ivory house" at Samaria) at the cost, in the biblical narrative's own sharply critical framing, of introducing rival cultic practice into the Israelite court.
entries.note: 1 Kings 16:31; Josephus, Antiquities 8.13.1–2, citing Menander of Ephesus on Ithobaal I of Tyre.

entries.label: Vassalage as a Survival Strategy
entries.hint: Both kingdoms spent most of their final two centuries as tribute-paying vassals of whichever regional power was ascendant — Assyria, then briefly Egypt, then Babylon — a diplomatic strategy that could preserve a subordinate kingdom's existence for generations but that collapsed disastrously whenever a king judged the moment right to rebel, as Hoshea did against Assyria in 722 BC and Zedekiah did against Babylon in 587 BC.
entries.note: Comparative pattern across 2 Kings 15–25 of tribute payment, vassal treaty, and rebellion cycles under Assyrian and Babylonian overlordship.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Caught between Egypt, Assyria and Babylon

entries.label: Between Egypt, Assyria and Babylon
entries.hint: Israel and Judah occupied the land bridge between Egypt and Mesopotamia, a position that brought trade and cultural contact but subjected both kingdoms, throughout their existence, to the ambitions of whichever great power dominated the corridor — Egyptian New Kingdom withdrawal enabled their emergence, Assyrian expansion ended Israel, and Egyptian-Babylonian rivalry over the corridor ultimately ended Judah, a geography of vulnerability neither kingdom's own military power could offset.
entries.note: Comparative geopolitical framing of Israel and Judah's position on the Via Maris/King's Highway corridor between Egyptian and Mesopotamian spheres of power, 1200–586 BC.

entries.label: Exile and an Open Question
entries.hint: The deportation of Judah's elite to Babylon ended the kingdom's political existence but did not end the community's identity, leaving its exiled and remaining population, priests and prophets to reckon with the apparent failure of the Davidic promise and Jerusalem's presumed inviolability — a theological and communal crisis whose resolution, and its transformative long-term consequences for how the tradition would be reshaped, unfolds in the following era rather than within this folio's own timeframe.
entries.note: 2 Kings 25:27–30 ends the narrative with Jehoiachin's release from Babylonian captivity in 561 BC, decades into the exile; the exile's full religious and literary consequences belong to the subsequent Persian-era history of the region.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A prophetess, and a city's last letters before the end

entries.label: Huldah the Prophetess
entries.hint: When Josiah's officials brought the newly discovered law scroll for authentication, they consulted not a priest but Huldah, a recognised prophetess living in Jerusalem's Second Quarter, whose oracle confirming the scroll's authority directly authorised the ensuing national reform — a documented instance of a woman holding the highest religious-interpretive authority in the kingdom at a pivotal constitutional moment.
entries.note: 2 Kings 22:14–20; 2 Chronicles 34:22–28.

entries.label: The Lachish Letters
entries.hint: A cache of ink-on-potsherd military correspondence, found in a burned guardroom at Lachish, records a garrison commander's urgent messages in the last months before Babylonian forces overran Judah's remaining fortified cities — one letter notes that the signal fires of nearby Azekah could no longer be seen, an eyewitness detail of a kingdom's defensive network failing in real time, independent of and consistent with the biblical account's own description of the same collapse.
entries.note: Lachish Letters (Ostraca), especially Letter IV, excavated 1935 (British Museum and Rockefeller Museum, Jerusalem), c.589–587 BC; compare Jeremiah 34:7 on Lachish and Azekah as Judah's last remaining fortified cities.
